title: Hepatitis A Basics

sections.heading: About hepatitis A
sections.text: The hepatitis A virus is highly contagious. People who get hepatitis A may feel sick for a few weeks or several months but usually recover completely and do not have lasting liver damage. In rare cases, hepatitis A can cause liver failure and even death. This is more common in older people and in people with other serious health issues, such as chronic liver disease.

sections.heading: About hepatitis A
sections.text: Since 2016, there have been outbreaks in multiple states caused by person-to-person transmission. These outbreaks have primarily been from person-to-person contact, especially among people who use drugs, people experiencing homelessness, and men who have sex with men.

sections.heading: Hepatitis A in 2023
sections.text: People aged 30–39 years had the highest rate of hepatitis A.

sections.heading: Hepatitis A in 2023
sections.text: From 2022 to 2023, there was a 28% decrease in the number of newly reported HAV cases.

sections.heading: Hepatitis A in 2023
sections.text: The number of hepatitis A cases in 2023 was 1.2 times as high as in 2015.

sections.heading: Hepatitis A in 2023
sections.text: The rate of hepatitis A among Hispanic people was 2.0 times as high as the rate of hepatitis A among non-Hispanic White people.

sections.heading: Signs and symptoms
sections.text: Not everyone with hepatitis A has symptoms. Adults are more likely to have symptoms than children. If symptoms develop, they usually appear 2–7 weeks after exposure. Symptoms usually last less than 2 months, although some people can feel sick for as long as 6 months.

sections.heading: Did you know?
sections.text: Symptoms can include:

sections.heading: Did you know?
sections.text: Dark urine or clay-colored stools

sections.heading: Did you know?
sections.text: Diarrhea

sections.heading: Did you know?
sections.text: Feeling tired

sections.heading: Did you know?
sections.text: Fever

sections.heading: Did you know?
sections.text: Joint pain

sections.heading: Did you know?
sections.text: Loss of appetite

sections.heading: Did you know?
sections.text: Nausea, stomach pain, throwing up

sections.heading: Did you know?
sections.text: Yellow skin or eyes (jaundice)

sections.heading: Did you know?
sections.text: Learn more about signs and symptoms of hepatitis A.

sections.heading: Risk factors
sections.text: Anyone who hasn’t been vaccinated or previously infected can get hepatitis A. Certain life circumstances and behaviors can also increase your risk of infection.

sections.heading: Risk factors
sections.text: Learn more about who is at risk for hepatitis A.

sections.heading: How it spreads
sections.text: Hepatitis A is spread when someone ingests the virus, even in very small amounts. This usually occurs through person-to-person contact or by eating or drinking contaminated food or drink.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.text: The best way to prevent hepatitis A is by getting vaccinated. You need to get all the shots in the series to be fully protected.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.text: CDC recommends the following groups get vaccinated against hepatitis A:

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.text: All children ages 12–23 months.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.text: All children and adolescents between ages 2–18 years who have not been vaccinated.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.text: All people, including pregnant women, with increased risk factors for hepatitis A.

sections.heading: Fact
sections.text: In addition, it’s important to practice good hand hygiene — including thoroughly washing hands after using the bathroom, changing diapers, and before preparing or eating food.

sections.heading: Fact
sections.text: Learn more about preventing hepatitis A.

sections.heading: Screening, testing, and diagnosis
sections.text: A doctor can give you a blood test if you think you have been exposed to HAV.

sections.heading: Treatment and recovery
sections.text: To treat the symptoms of hepatitis A, doctors usually recommend resting, eating a well-balanced diet, and making sure you get enough fluids.

sections.heading: Clarifying misconceptions
sections.text: Hepatitis A is sometimes difficult to understand, especially how it spreads and how people recover. Here are a few misconceptions cleared up for you.

sections.heading: "If I don’t have symptoms, I’m not infected."
sections.text: Many people with hepatitis A do not have any symptoms. Young children are more likely than adults to have hepatitis A without symptoms.

sections.heading: "If I don’t have symptoms, I can’t spread the virus to others."
sections.text: You can still spread HAV to others even if you don’t have any symptoms. It’s possible to spread HAV up to 2 weeks before you have any symptoms.

sections.heading: "I can get infected with HAV more than once."
sections.text: If you have been infected with HAV in the past, you can’t get infected again. Once you recover from hepatitis A, you develop antibodies that protect you from reinfection.

sections.heading: What to expect long-term
sections.text: People who get hepatitis A may feel sick for a few weeks or several months but usually recover completely and do not have lasting liver damage.

sections.heading: What CDC is doing
sections.text: CDC supports health departments that conduct viral hepatitis A outbreak response and tracking.

sections.heading: What CDC is doing
sections.text: Since 2016, CDC has provided guidance and support to 37 states that have reported person-to-person outbreaks of hepatitis A. To assist with outbreak investigations, CDC sent disease intervention specialists, epidemiologists, lab experts, and public health advisors to nine states.

sections.heading: What CDC is doing
sections.text: CDC continues to support vaccine supply and vaccine policy development.
